title: distinct identities: minority women in u.s. politics . edited by nadia e. brown and sarah allen gershon. new york: routledge, 2016.
display_name: Distinct Identities: Minority Women in U.S. Politics. Edited by Nadia E. Brown and Sarah Allen Gershon. New York: Routledge, 2016.
abstract: previous articlenext article freebook reviewdistinct identities: minority women in u.s. politics. edited by nadia e. brown and sarah allen gershon. new york: routledge, 2016.tony e. carey jr.tony e. carey jr.university of north texas search for more articles by this author pdfpdf plusfull text add to favoritesdownload citationtrack citationspermissionsreprints share onfacebooktwitterlinked inredditemailqr code sectionsmoreminority politics and gender politics are burgeoning subfields in political science. increasingly, work in both areas is represented in the top political science journals, suggesting that they enjoy broader acceptance within the discipline as legitimate areas of inquiry. while these are positive steps, researchers of intersectionality contend that the study of race or gender in isolation overshadows the ways in which the influence of either race or gender on experiences and life outcomes are compounded by other intersecting identities (crenshaw 1989). while the theoretical literature on intersectionality within political science is rich, empirical approaches have been sparse, although growing in number (hancock 2007).brown and gershon s collection highlights advances in the study of intersectionality as well as some of its challenges. the volume is separated into three sections. the first section focuses on how overlapping racial and gender identities operate within the mass public. the chapters within this section explore how resources shape political participation differently across racial and gender groups (holman, chap. 2), gender differences in attitudes about gender equality between native-born blacks and black caribbean immigrants (caper and smith, chap. 3), the ways that black women perceive and respond to racial inequality (dowe, chap. 4), the political behavior of asian american women (harvie, chap. 5), and differences in attitudes toward military intervention in iraq between latinas and latinos (vansickle-ward and pantoja, chap. 6). caper and smith s chapter on the influence of black racial identification, ethnicity, and gender on attitudes about gender equality is particularly compelling. the authors discover that while the gender attitudes of black immigrants and black american men are shaped by their racial identification, black american women s attitudes toward gender equality are not influenced by their racial attachment. caper and smith argue that the absence of a relationship suggests that black women s attitudes toward gender equality are informed by a more gender-oriented racial consciousness.the second section addresses how the racial and gender identities of minority women candidates influence how they campaign for office. chapters within this section address the trait attributions and perceived electability of black female candidates (carew, chap. 7), how voters of south asian descent negotiate their religious and ethnic identities when evaluating south asian american women candidates (sriram, chap. 8), and the stereotypes surrounding the policy competencies of latina candidates (cargile, chap. 9). in this section, carew s contribution on the candidate stereotyping of black female candidates is particularly illuminating (carew, chap. 7). the presumption of intersectionality research is that black women are doubly disadvantaged by both their racial and gender identities. consequently, they should experience more negative trait attributions and lower perceived electability among voters. interestingly, the author discovers that participants report more positive attributions of black women than both white male and white female candidates. based on these results, one may conclude that black female candidates are stronger candidates for higher office than intersectionality research proposes. however, when asked to evaluate the dark-skinned black female candidate s electability and likelihood of winning, participants assessed her as the least electable and least likely winner. carew proposes two reasons for why she observes the relationships that she does in the study. first, black female candidates are perceived to be the most liberal among white male, white female, and black male candidates. therefore, the aversion to black female candidates may be because they are perceived to be more ideologically extreme than other candidates. second, dark skin may serve as a racial cue that motivates self-monitoring. carew provides suggestive evidence of this conclusion by comparing participants evaluations of a hypothetical light-skinned black woman candidate to the dark-skinned black woman candidate. the fair-skinned black female candidate was evaluated more negatively, yet she was perceived as more electable and more likely to win than the dark-skinned candidate. carew s chapter concentrates on another dimension of intersectionality (i.e., skin complexion), but it also demonstrates that the consequences of these intersections may function differently than the theory suggests.finally, the third section of the volume highlights the complexities of holding elected office as a woman of color. this section of the edited volume contains more content than the other portions of the book. the contributions in this section examine how the media frames the campaigns of black women running for seats in the house of representatives (ward, chap. 10), the career pathways of women of color who run for state executive offices (sanbonmatsu, chap. 11), state-level factors that shape political office-holding among latinas (bejarano, chap. 12), the career paths of latinas in state legislatures (ramirez and burlingame, chap. 13), the career histories of asian pacific american women winning local, state, and national offices (filler and lien, chap. 14), media depictions of the first lady of the united states, michelle obama (gillespie, chap. 15), the presidential candidacies of two black women candidates, charlene mitchell and shirley chisholm (greer, chap. 16), the structural, institutional, and cultural barriers that limit the rise of indigenous women to tribal leadership positions (prindeville and broxton, chap. 17), and, finally, differences in the legislative behavior of black male and female state legislators surrounding abortion policy (williams, chap. 18). among these chapters, ramirez and burlingame s chapter stands out. the authors seek to explain the smaller disparity in descriptive representation that exists between latinos and latinas than men and women in other racial groups. they trace the career path of latina legislators to explain their greater electoral success. in particular, they are interested in whether latina candidates for state legislatures are more likely to have political experience prior to running for office. ramirez and burlingame discover that latinas were less likely to have prior political experience than their male counterparts. they interpret this finding as evidence that latinas do not need political experience at the local level to win seats to the state legislature. the chapter suggests that local-level offices may not offer the upward mobility to female candidates of color that they do for other candidates.overall, distinct identities makes several contributions to our understanding of the evaluation of minority female candidates. brown and gershon have organized the volume thoughtfully to address each stage of a candidacy, from recruitment, to campaigning, to governance. this thematic approach is important because previous studies reveal that the challenges faced by women candidates emerge long before they run for public office (fox and oxley 2003; green 2003; sanbonmatsu 2002). in addition, although most of the intersectional literature focuses on race, gender, and class, several chapters employ other group identities, such as ethnicity (caper and smith, chap. 3) and religious affiliation (sriram, chap. 8). ultimately, the book offers a thorough treatment of intersectionality that provides the reader an accurate glimpse of the current status of the subfield within political science.while acknowledging its contributions, the volume also has its shortcomings. the first weakness involves the research approach represented in the volume. each chapter focuses on the identities of candidates or the mass public in isolation; however, the most promising contributions are likely to explore the interaction between candidates and the individuals who evaluate them. the remaining criticisms address more general concerns about intersectionality research that are reflected in the volume. given the nature of the subfield, studies of intersectionality often lack parsimony. instead, they tend to funnel down to greater levels of specificity. while it is important to account for different life experiences, it also limits the ability of intersectionality research to reach unified theories. a related complication of intersectionality research, particularly quantitatively oriented research, is that it typically requires greater complexity within the research design and analysis. specifically, these studies demand two and, in some cases, multiple interactions between different variables to properly capture intersectional relationships. however, these interaction terms can become unwieldy quickly.despite these concerns, brown and gershon s edited volume is a valuable resource for scholars of identity politics, particularly gender politics and racial and ethnic politics. additionally, distinct identities will be a valuable text for graduate and upper-level undergraduate courses.referencescrenshaw, kimberle w. 1989. demarginalizing the intersection of race and sex: a black feminist title: whose knowledge, whose nature? biodiversity, conservation, and the political ecology of social movements
display_name: Whose Knowledge, Whose nature? Biodiversity, Conservation, and the Political Ecology of Social Movements
abstract: this paper proposes a framework for rethinking the conservation and appropriation of biological diversity from the perspective of social movements. it argues that biodiversity, although with concrete biophysical referents, is a discourse of recent origin. this discourse fosters a complex network of diverse actors, from international organizations and ngos to local communities and social movements. four views of biodiversity produced by this network (centered on global resource management, national sovereignity, biodemocracy, and cultural autonomy, respectively) are discussed in the first part of the paper. the second part focuses on the cultural autonomy perspective developed by social movements. it examines in detail the rise and development of the social movement of black communities in the pacific rainforest region of colombia. this movement, it is argued, articulates through their practice an entire political ecology of sustainability and conservation. the main elements of this political ecology are discussed and presented as a viable alternative to dominant frameworks. key words: political ecology, social movements, rainforest, biodiversity, afrocolombians, global networks.

title: racial disparities in health and health behaviors among gay, lesbian, bisexual and heterosexual men and women in the brfss-sop
display_name: Racial disparities in health and health behaviors among gay, lesbian, bisexual and heterosexual men and women in the BRFSS-SOP
abstract: objectives: research on sexual minority health lack examinations of how sexual orientation intersects with other identities, including racial/ethnic identity, to shape health outcomes among u.s. adults. this study examines how health status and health behavior varies for gay, lesbian, and bisexual men and women who identify as non-hispanic white, non-hispanic black, latino, asian/pacific islander, and american indian/alaskan native. by examining health and health behaviors within and across sexual minority subgroups, our study reports on race/ethnic, gender, and sexual orientation specific health risks. methods: we respond to shortcomings in current data by utilizing aggregated data from fourteen states from the behavioral risk factor surveillance system (brfss) collected between 2005 and 2010 ( n = 557,773). we investigated the odds of reporting poorer health, current cigarette smoking, and obesity by sexual orientation within race/ethnic and gender subgroups; all statistical analyses were performed in 2016. results: results suggest persistent health and behavior disadvantages for lesbian and bisexual women of all racial and ethnic identities, relative to heterosexuals. some of the heightened odds are extreme. asian/pacific islander lesbian (or = 3.92) and bisexual (or = 4.61) women, for example, have 4.0 times higher odds of smoking than heterosexual a/pi women. results for men are more variable. to illustrate, the odds of obesity for white and a/pi men are indistinguishable between bisexuals and heterosexuals, and black and american indian/alaskan native bisexuals have lower odds of obesity than their heterosexual counterparts. conclusion: these findings highlight the need for policy efforts aimed at improving health and health behaviors among lesbian and bisexual women across groups, and more targeted efforts among sexual minority men.

title: something of collaborative manufacture
display_name: Something of Collaborative Manufacture
abstract: using qualitative data, this article documents how organizations contribute to the construction of their members race and gender identities. data collection took place in four organizations, from a small nonprofit to a large financial services firm. using interactions as the unit of analysis, the author compiled and investigated a database of 114 interactions, creating a process model of how working in an organization can spotlight and change the expression of racial, ethnic, and gender identities. the article makes four contributions: it suggests a broader reach for organizational influence on individual identity, since earlier research has explored work-related identities; it distinguishes among levels of influence by isolating the discrete role of interpersonal encounters, organizational practices, and the combination of the two; it casts light on how identity construction happens even without intentional effort by individuals or organizations; and it illustrates the importance of modest changes in the construction of identity.

title: critical incidents in the development of (multi)ethnic-racial identity: experiences of individuals with mixed ethnic-racial backgrounds in the u.s.
display_name: Critical incidents in the development of (multi)ethnic-racial identity: Experiences of individuals with mixed ethnic-racial backgrounds in the U.S.
abstract: secure ethnic-racial identity (eri) is tied to well-being, especially for minority individuals; however, there is still little consensus on the key processes and optimal outcomes of various multiethnic-racial (me-r; i.e., individuals with parents from different ethnic-racial groups) identity development models. in this study, we examine the critical incidents in personal and social relationships that are central to me-r identity development. twenty-nine me-r individuals provided retrospective accounts of incidents and conversations they self-perceived to be critical to their eri development. four major themes emerged: incidents and conversations surrounding intergroup contact, confrontation, heritage, and appearance were all recalled as critical to me-r identity development. these findings highlight the importance of studying the ways that eri is constituted through interaction with others. implications and directions for future research are discussed.
